title: Welcome to Lilith University
subtitle: A very short guide to finding, getting, studying and making courses
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A four-chapter orientation to Lilith University and the Lilith Learning Lab app: what a course is, how to find and download one, how to study a chapter with quizzes, flashcards and labs, and how to build and share your own course.

summary: Lilith University is a free library of self-study courses. Each course is one file that you download once and then use offline in the Lilith Learning Lab app.
The website lets you search and read each course outline before you download it. The app holds your courses, shows lessons, reads them aloud with the Teacher, and runs the labs on your own device.
There are no accounts, no tracking and no payments. Your progress stays on your device.

items: ELI5. Lilith University is a big shelf of little books. You pick one, take it home, and read it anywhere, even with no internet.

Lilith University is a catalog of courses you can study at your own pace. Think of the website as a course shelf and the Lilith Learning Lab app as your desk. On the shelf you read what each course covers. At your desk you actually learn it.

A course is a single file. It holds chapters, and each chapter holds a lesson, a short quiz, flashcards and labs. Once the file is on your phone, nothing more needs to be downloaded, so you can study on a train or a plane.

The catalog groups courses by category, such as Mathematics, Computer Science, Languages, and Hardware and Embedded. Each course also has a level, from beginner to advanced, and tags that help search. Start with a level that matches what you already know.

summary: Open Library, then Browse online in the app. Search by name or tag, filter by category, and read the chapter outline. Tap Get to download a course into your library.
You can also import a course file that someone sent you. Courses are plain JSON files, so they can be shared like any other file.
Start with the level that fits you, and look at the outline first: a good course shows its chapters in a sensible order, from basics up.

items: ELI5. Finding a course is like searching a toy shop: type what you want, pick a shelf, peek inside, then take it.
To find a course, open Browse online. Type a word like python or hebrew into the search box. The results shrink as you type. You can also pick a category to see only that group.

Tap a course to read its outline before you commit. The outline lists every chapter, so you can see whether it starts where you need it to. When you are happy, tap Get. The app downloads the file and puts it in your library.

If a friend sends you a course file, use Import and choose the file. The course appears in your library like any other. Courses are stored on your device, so deleting one frees space, and you can download it again whenever you like.

chapters.title: How to study a chapter
summary: Each chapter has the same shape: a short lesson, a quiz, flashcards and labs. Read or listen to the lesson, answer the quiz, then do the labs, which turn ideas into skill.
Flashcards work best in short daily sessions. Seeing a card again after a day, then three days, then a week, makes it stick.
Do not skip the labs. Typing a line of code or putting steps in order shows you what you really understand.

glossary.def: The explanation at the start of a chapter.
A few questions that check what you just learned.
Question and answer cards for quick review.
Reviewing material at growing gaps so it is remembered longer.

keyPoints: Lesson, quiz, cards, labs: the same loop every chapter.
Short daily sessions beat one long one.
Listen with the Teacher when your eyes are busy.

items: ELI5. Learning sticks when you hear it, answer it, and then do it. Like learning to ride a bike: listen, wobble, ride.

Every chapter follows one loop. First the lesson explains an idea in plain words. Then the quiz asks a few questions, so you notice what did not stick. The flashcards fix the details, and the labs let you use the idea with your hands.

A simple plan is twenty minutes a day. Listen to the lesson, answer the quiz, and do one lab. The next day, start with the flashcards from yesterday. Review old cards at growing gaps: one day, three days, one week. This is called spaced repetition and it beats cramming.
Mistakes are useful. A wrong quiz answer tells you which part to reread, and a failed lab shows you exactly what you misunderstood. When the course ends, take the final exam to see the whole picture.

practice.title: Review days
practice.intro: Write review_days(start, gaps). Given the first study day (an integer) and a list of gaps in days, return the list of review days, each gap counted from the previous review. For start 0 and gaps [1, 2, 4] the days are 1, 3 and 7.
practice.solution:
def review_days(start, gaps):
    days = []
    day = start
    for g in gaps:
        day = day + g
        days.append(day)
    return days

summary: Anyone can write a course. A course is a JSON file in the lilith-course format, and the web editor lets you build one without writing JSON by hand.
Each chapter needs a title, a lesson, a few quiz questions and cards. Labs can be fill-in-the-blank, matching, ordering, Python code, a terminal, or a small web app.
Export your file and import it in the app to try it. If it is good, share it so others can learn from it.

items: ELI5. A course is just a notebook with a special shape. If you fill in the shape, you can lend your notebook to anyone.

A course is plain text in a format called JSON. It lists chapters, and each chapter has a title, a summary, a lesson, quiz questions, flashcards and labs. You do not have to write this by hand, because the editor on the Lilith University site gives you forms for everything.

The lab types give you variety. A fill lab blanks out words, a match lab pairs items, an order lab sorts steps, and a Python lab runs your code against tests. A terminal lab simulates a command line, and a web app lab can hold a small interactive tool.

Start small. Make one chapter, export the file, and import it into the app. Fix what feels awkward, add the next chapter, and repeat. When a course is ready, share the file, and it works the same on every device.
